events.title: Nine o'clock
events.body: The rectory has four bedrooms and two priests, and after nine it has one, because {@pastor} goes up early and closes his door and the house belongs to the television and the hum of the refrigerator. You have said the evening Mass, eaten what was left in the oven, returned the calls that could be returned. It is a Tuesday in {parish} and there is nothing more to do until morning, which is the thing nobody warned you about. In the seminary there was always a corridor. Here the corridor is a hallway with a closed door at the end of it, and the parish, which loves you or is deciding whether to, is asleep in two thousand houses you can see from the window. The phone would work. There are men from the class you could call, and one or two who would pick up. There is the breviary on the desk, open to Night Prayer, which you have not said. There is the quiet, which is not the same as peace, and which you are beginning to understand you will have to learn to live inside, or find some way to fill, and that both of those are choices with a shape.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest alone in a rectory on an ordinary weeknight. Domestic detail, no self-pity. The loneliness is structural, not a crisis.

choices.label: Call {@closest_classmate}
choices.outcome: He picks up on the fourth ring, in a rectory forty miles away that sounds exactly like yours. You talk for an hour about nothing: his pastor's cooking, your pastor's television, a funeral director you both know. Neither of you says the word for what the call is for. You hang up lighter, and you notice you have already started to think of Tuesday as the night you call.

choices.label: Say Night Prayer, slowly, and go up
choices.outcome: You say it at the desk with the lamp on, the short psalm and the Nunc Dimittis and the antiphon to Our Lady, and it takes nine minutes, and when it is over the house is exactly as quiet as before. But the quiet has an address now. It is the quiet you are supposed to be in. You go up. You do not sleep at once, and that is all right.

choices.label: Knock on the closed door at the end of the hall
choices.outcome: {@pastor} is in a chair with a book and reading glasses, and he looks up as if he had been expecting this for some weeks. He says come in. He does not ask what is wrong. He tells you about his own first rectory, and the pastor who never spoke to him, and says that he had decided not to be that man and then had mostly forgotten to check. You talk until eleven.

choices.label: Fill it: take the Wednesday holy hour, the youth group, the hospital rota, until there is no nine o'clock
choices.outcome: Within a month you are out five evenings in seven. The parish notices and approves; the young priest is everywhere. You are good at it, and you are tired, and the quiet is still there when you come in at ten, only now you are too spent to hear it. That is a solution. It is not the only one, and it has a bill that has not yet been presented.

events.title: The last of your friends
events.body: The invitation is thick and cream-colored and addressed to you without the title, which he would have done on purpose. He is the last of the friends from before, the one who drove you to the seminary the first day and said nothing sentimental and then called every few months for seven years. The wedding is a Saturday at four, at a vineyard two hours away, and the officiant is a friend of the bride's with a certificate from the internet. He knows what you can and cannot do; he has read up on it, which is like him. He is not asking you to marry them. He is asking you to stand up with him, and afterward, at the dinner, to say something, a blessing, whatever you like. He says he knows Saturday is a work day. He says he would understand. You look at the calendar. There is the five o'clock vigil, which you could ask {@pastor} to take, and there is the fact that he is the last one, and that after this he will have a wife and a house and the phone will ring less, as it should, and you will be the friend who is a priest.
events.flavorPrompt: An old friend marrying civilly, asking his priest friend to stand up with him. Warm, exact about what a priest can and cannot do at a wedding outside the Church. No lecture.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} for the Saturday, and stand up with him in a suit
choices.outcome: {@pastor} takes the vigil without comment, which is its own comment. You stand beside your friend in a suit and not the collar, and you do not say the words that are not yours to say, and at dinner you give a blessing that you wrote in the car, and it lands. Driving home at midnight you are happier and lonelier than you have been in a year, and you understand that these will keep arriving together.

choices.label: Go in the collar, sit in the second row, and leave before the dancing
choices.outcome: You drive up after the noon Mass and arrive with ten minutes to spare. You sit where he can see you. You shake the bride's hand and her mother's, who is thrilled to have a priest at the wedding and tells you so twice. You are back for the vigil with a boutonnière still on. He texts you at one in the morning to say thank you for coming, and you know that you were there and also that you were not.

choices.label: Tell him exactly what you can do, and offer to convalidate it in a church when they are ready
choices.outcome: You explain it over the phone: that you can come and be glad, that you cannot witness a marriage the Church does not recognize, and that the door is not closed, because a convalidation is a real thing with a real rite, and you would be the one to do it. He is quiet and then says he did not know that was possible. Whether it happens is theirs. The offer is yours, and it is honest, and it costs you the toast.

choices.label: Send a gift and a long letter, and take the vigil yourself
choices.outcome: The letter is the best thing you have written that year and he will keep it, and it is not the same as being there, and both of you know it. You say the vigil Mass to a half-full church and preach well. He does not call less, exactly. He calls differently. You have chosen the parish over the last of the old life, and it was probably the right choice, and it was a choice.

events.title: Thursday evenings
events.body: She runs the adult faith formation on Thursday evenings, which you were given because {@pastor} did not want it, and which has become the best hour of your week. She is married, and her husband travels, and her questions are the real ones, the ones you came to the priesthood to answer, and she stays after to ask them while the chairs are being stacked. None of this is anything. You have said that to yourself in the car every Thursday for two months. What you have not said is that you dress differently on Thursdays, that you have begun to prepare the session with her in mind, that when she missed a week you were angry at the empty chair, and that you know the name of the town her husband is in this week and when he comes back. You are not in love. You are a man who has noticed that he has begun to count the days to Thursday, and who knows from the whole literature of his own formation exactly what that means and what it becomes if it is left alone. Nothing has happened. That is the moment this is for.
events.flavorPrompt: Interior, honest, unsensational. A married parishioner, a real friendship, and a priest who has caught himself early. The choice is about what to do before anything happens.

choices.label: Take it to your confessor this week, all of it, including the town and the day
choices.outcome: He listens to the whole of it and does not treat it as a crime or as nothing. He asks whether you have told her anything, and you say no, and he says then the thing is still yours to decide, and that you must decide it before you talk to her again. You leave with a rule: the sessions continue, the staying after does not, and you tell him each month whether you have kept it.

choices.label: Hand the Thursday group to {@dre} and give no reason
choices.outcome: {@dre} takes it with a look, because the group was going well and there is no reason on the face of it. Attendance falls by a third. She writes you a short note asking if she did something wrong, and you write back that she did not, which is true and is not the whole truth. You have removed yourself from the thing. You have not yet understood it, and it will find another Thursday.

choices.label: Keep the group, keep the friendship, and manage it yourself
choices.outcome: You are careful. You leave with the others, you answer the questions in the room and not after it, you stop knowing where her husband is. It works, mostly. What you have not done is tell anyone, and the thing that is not told has a way of keeping its own counsel. Some Thursdays are easy. Some Thursdays you sit in the car afterward for a long time before starting the engine.

effects.value: an attachment to a married parishioner, managed alone and never brought to direction

choices.label: Tell her, so that at least one thing between you is true
choices.outcome: You say it in the emptied hall in two sentences, that you have come to care for her in a way you must not, and that you are telling her so that you will have to stop. She is kind and shaken and says she had wondered. She does not come back to the group. You were honest, and you have also placed a thing in another person's keeping that is now hers to carry, or repeat, or misremember.

effects.value: told a married parishioner of his attraction to her

events.title: The youth minister
events.body: {@pastor} hired the youth minister last spring, part-time, out of a line in the budget that had been empty for six years, and she is good: the Sunday night group has doubled, the parents like her, and she and you have built the thing together out of nothing, which is the kind of work that makes people close. She is not married. She is a few years younger than you. You have started to eat lunch in the office on the days she is in, and she has started to bring two coffees. On Sunday night, stacking chairs, she said something about the two of you that was a joke and was not, and you laughed, and neither of you looked at the other for a while afterward. The difference between this and the other kind of trouble is that this one is mutual and this one is seen. {@secretary} has noticed the coffees. The teenagers, who notice everything, have a name for the two of you that you were not meant to hear. You are her supervisor, on paper. Nothing has happened, and both of you know that nothing is not the word for it.
events.flavorPrompt: Mutual, unspoken attraction between a young priest and a lay colleague he supervises, visible to the staff. The stakes are professional and public as well as interior.

choices.label: Move her reporting line to {@pastor} and take yourself off the Sunday group
choices.outcome: You do it as a paperwork question: the pastor should supervise paid staff, you say, and the vicar should not be the only adult at the Sunday group. {@pastor} agrees without asking why, which means he knows. The coffees stop because there is no longer a reason for them. It is clean. It is also the end of the best working partnership you have had, and she understood exactly what it was.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} what is happening, before {@secretary} does
choices.outcome: You say it in his office with the door shut: that there is a thing between you and the youth minister, that nothing has happened, and that you would rather he heard it from you. He is quiet and then says that he had two years like that once and nobody told him anything, and that it was worse. He takes the supervision himself. The staff draw their own conclusions, but they draw them about a thing that was handled.

choices.label: Change nothing. You are adults, and the work is good.
choices.outcome: The work stays good. The Sunday group grows. So does the thing in the office, which is now the parish's open secret, and the parish, which loves a story, begins to tell it. {@secretary} says something to {@pastor}. A parent says something to {@secretary}. Nothing has happened, and you have let the appearance of it become the most interesting fact about you in {parish}, which is a kind of thing happening.

effects.value: a visible closeness with a lay staff member he supervised, talked about in the parish

choices.label: Say it to her plainly, once, and then draw the line where it has to be
choices.outcome: You say it on a Tuesday in the empty hall: that you have felt what she has, that it cannot go anywhere, and that you would rather say so than let it be a thing the two of you manage by not looking. She says thank you and then that she is going to look for another parish, and she does, within the year. It was the honest thing. The Sunday group is smaller now. You do not eat lunch in the office.

events.title: The cabinet
events.body: The cabinet in the rectory sitting room was stocked by a pastor three pastors ago and has been kept up since by grateful parishioners, funeral directors, and the Knights, and it is, by any standard, a good cabinet. {@pastor} has a drink at nine. Not two; one, poured with care, in the same chair, with the news on, and for the first month he did not offer, and then one night he did, and now the second glass is on the tray before you come down. He is not a drunk. He is a man who has lived alone for thirty years and has found one thing that marks the end of the day, and he would like company for it, and the company he would like is you. It is the friendliest he has been. You know what a full cabinet and a lonely pastor are, because it was in the material at every stage of formation and because, if you are honest, you know it from before that. Nine o'clock is coming. He will pour, and he will not ask, and he will be hurt, quietly, if the glass sits there, and you will have to decide what the glass is.
events.flavorPrompt: A lonely pastor's nightly ritual and a young priest invited into it. The cabinet is a fact of rectory life, not a villain. For a player in recovery, the stakes are total and unspoken.

choices.label: Take the glass. One, with him, at nine.
choices.outcome: It becomes the best half hour of the day in that house. At nine he talks; you learn the diocese from him, the bishops he has outlived, the men who were ruined and how. One glass. Then, some nights, the second, because the story is not finished. You are not a drunk either. You are a man with a nightly drink in a house where there is nothing else to mark the day, which is how it starts for everyone it starts for.

effects.value: a nightly drink with the pastor, become a habit

choices.label: Take the glass, and tell yourself it has been long enough that one is one
choices.outcome: One is one for eleven days. Then it is the second, and then it is the one you pour yourself after he has gone up, because the cabinet is right there and nobody counts it, and you know within a month, with the old exact knowledge, where you are. He does not notice. He would not. The number you kept for years is gone, and no one in {diocese} knows there was a number.

effects.value: drinking again, alone, in the rectory, after years of sobriety

choices.label: Tell him you do not drink, and why, and ask him not to pour
choices.outcome: You say it in a sentence before he reaches the tray. He stops with the bottle in his hand and looks at you for a while and then puts it back and says he is sorry, he did not know, and he did not. He pours his own and you sit with a coffee and the news, and it is nearly the same. Within the month you have found the Tuesday meeting in the next town, and he has noticed you go, and said nothing, kindly.

choices.label: Sit with him at nine with a glass of soda water, and give no reason
choices.outcome: He notices, the first night, and the second, and on the third he stops putting the second glass out and starts putting out a bottle of the sparkling water the housekeeper buys. He never asks. You keep the half hour, which was the thing he wanted. You have given him the company and kept the rest, and there is a small, permanent reserve in the room that both of you have agreed not to name.

events.title: Eleven in six weeks
events.body: The first one was in the second week of January and the eleventh is on Thursday, and in between you have learned the funeral director's coffee order, the difference between the three cemeteries, and which of the readings the families always choose. {@pastor} has taken none of them. He does not say why; the parish assumes he is old, and he lets it. You have preached eleven times about the resurrection of the body to people who did not want theology, they wanted their mother back, and you have stood at eleven gravesides in a coat that is not warm enough, and you have gone from the committal to the noon Mass without eating. You are not grieving. You did not know most of them. You are something else, which is that the words have started to come out of you in the same order every time, and that on Tuesday, at the vigil, you looked at the family in the front row and felt nothing, and noticed that you felt nothing, and preached anyway, and that it was fine. Thursday's family has asked for a meeting about the homily.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest at the end of a run of winter funerals: numb, competent, and beginning to hear himself repeat. The pastor has quietly left them all to him.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to take Thursday, and the next two
choices.outcome: He says yes in a way that makes clear he had been waiting to be asked and would never have offered. He takes Thursday and preaches badly and the family does not care, because he is the pastor and he came. You sleep for eleven hours. It was the right ask. It was also the first time you have asked him for anything, and he has filed it, and he will mention it in some other context, months from now, when it suits him.

choices.label: Preach the same homily on Thursday. It was a good homily. Nobody will know.
choices.outcome: Nobody knows. It is a good homily, and the family cries in the right place, and the funeral director says afterward that you have a gift. You go from the cemetery to the noon Mass and preach the homily you preached last year. Something has been set down that you will have to decide, some other week, whether to pick back up. For now it is warm in the car, and there is Friday's to write, or not.

choices.label: Write Thursday's fresh, and Friday's, and take the meeting, and keep going
choices.outcome: You write it at midnight and it is good, and the meeting with the family goes well, and you take the twelfth and the thirteenth, and the parish begins to say the young priest is the one you want for a funeral. {@pastor} says nothing. You are running on something that is not rest, and it is working, and there is a bill for it that has not yet been presented and that will not be presented to you first.

choices.label: Go back to the vigil for each of them: the rosary, the family, the hour before, and say Mass for the eleven on Saturday
choices.outcome: You take the eleven names to the chapel and say the Mass for them alone on a Saturday morning, and it takes as long as it takes. It does not make you less tired. It makes the tiredness belong to someone. Thursday's homily is not the same as Tuesday's, because you have remembered who they were, and the family's meeting is about something else by the time it happens.

events.title: A year without weather
events.body: It was last Lent that you noticed, and it is Lent again, so it has been a year. The hour is still there. You go to the chapel at six and sit before the tabernacle and say the Office and then sit, and for a year nothing has come back. Not doubt; doubt would be something. Not distraction, which you know how to fight. The absence of anything. The words of the psalms go past like a train you are not on. You have said Mass every day of that year and consecrated bread and wine and believed, in the sense that you have not stopped believing, and the belief has had no temperature at all. You know the names for this. You were taught them in a course on the spiritual life by a man who had read Saint John of the Cross and, you suspected even then, had not experienced him. The names are consoling for about a week. After that you are a man who goes to a room every morning to meet someone who has not, for a year, arrived, and who has begun to wonder whether he ever did, or whether the years of warmth were a young man's temperament and this is the truth.
events.flavorPrompt: Spiritual dryness, one year in, in Lent. Not a crisis of belief; the absence of feeling. The player's piety decides whether he can read it as the dark night or must read it as nothing.

choices.label: Read it as the dark night, and keep the hour as if He were there
choices.outcome: You decide, because it is a decision, that the absence is a presence you have not learned to read. You keep the hour. You stop asking it to feel like anything. Somewhere past Easter, not in a moment you could point to, the psalms are addressed to someone again. You will never be sure it was not simply the season turning. You are sure that you kept the appointment, and that this was the whole of what was asked.

choices.label: Admit that it was never much, and stop calling the hour prayer
choices.outcome: You had suspected it for longer than a year. You say the Office because you are bound to, and you say Mass because it is the work, and you stop sitting in the chapel pretending that the sitting is something. It is honest. It is also the first time you have said, even to yourself, that the interior life the priesthood assumes may not, in your case, be there, and that you are a priest anyway, and you do not know yet what that makes you.

choices.label: Cut the hour to twenty minutes and give the rest to the parish
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes is what the parish gets from its other priest, and the forty you free go to the hospital list and the school, and the parish is better for it, measurably. The twenty minutes are as dry as the sixty were. You have made a practical decision about an impractical thing, and it will be a long time before you know whether it was a wise one or the first step down a well-worn road.

choices.label: Keep the hour as a discipline, and refuse to interpret it either way
choices.outcome: You go on going. You do not decide it is the dark night and you do not decide it is nothing; you decide that a man who has promised to pray prays, and that what it feels like is not his business. It is the least dramatic answer and the hardest to keep. In the summer, at a funeral, the words of the preface catch in your throat for no reason, and you do not make anything of it, and you notice.

events.title: The book on the nightstand
events.body: It was not a dramatic book. It was a careful one, by a man who had been a believer and who wrote without contempt, and you read it because you read everything, and you finished it at two in the morning on a Wednesday and lay in the dark and found that the argument had gone in and was not coming out. It is not that you think he is right. It is that you cannot, lying there, say why he is wrong, and you have spent your life being the man who could say why. On Sunday you will stand at the ambo and lead two thousand people in the Creed, and every clause of it is a claim about what is the case, and you will say it in the first person. You have been trained to distinguish between faith and feeling, between assent and certainty, and the distinctions are good, and at two in the morning they are words. You know men who stopped asking. You know men who never started. You have always thought both of them were cheating, and now you are not sure that the ones who stopped were not simply tired, and you are tired. The book is still on the nightstand.
events.flavorPrompt: Intellectual doubt: an honest argument the priest cannot answer, and the Creed on Sunday. Register of a serious mind in trouble. No easy apologetics; no sneer at faith either.

choices.label: Take the argument apart the way you were trained to, for as long as it takes
choices.outcome: It takes three months and most of your free evenings. You read the answers and the answers to the answers, Newman on assent, the modern people, and at the end you have a position you can defend, which is not the same as the untroubled thing you had before. The Creed is harder to say now and truer, in the way that a thing chosen is truer than a thing inherited. The book stays on the shelf. You are not afraid of it.

choices.label: Take the book to someone who has been here, and say the Creed in the meantime
choices.outcome: The old priest you take it to has read it, and says so, and says he could not answer it either, at your age, and that what he did was keep saying Mass. You are not sure that is an answer. You are sure it is a life. You say the Creed on Sunday in the first person, and it costs something to say it, and you have begun to suspect that the cost is not a sign of dishonesty but of the thing finally weighing what it should.

choices.label: Put the book in a box in the basement and stop reading that kind of thing
choices.outcome: It works, in the sense that the argument fades if it is not fed, and the Creed comes easier by Easter. It costs you a thing you used to be proud of, which is that you would read anything. You catch yourself, in a homily, saying that some questions are not worth asking, and you hear it, and the man you were at twenty-five would have crossed the street to avoid the man who said it.

choices.label: Stop saying in the first person what you cannot say honestly, and tell the bishop
choices.outcome: You give it a year, because a year is fair, and at the end of the year you can say the Creed but not in the first person, and you decide that a priest who cannot is not one. You tell {@bishop} yourself. He does not argue theology with you, which you respect. You ask for the dispensation and it is, eventually, granted. You keep the book.

effects.value: He left the priesthood in his early years as a parochial vicar because he could no longer say the Creed in the first person and would not say it in any other. The bishop granted him a leave, and Rome, in time, the dispensation. He taught afterward, and read everything, and never spoke of the Church with contempt, which surprised the people who expected it.

events.title: Personal reasons
events.body: The letter was read at every Mass in a parish across {diocese} on a Sunday in October: the pastor there has stepped down for personal reasons, and the faithful are asked to pray for him. You know what the personal reasons are, because a woman from that parish came to {parish} for confession in the spring and then, outside the confessional, to talk, and what she told you about her son and that priest you carried to {@vicar_for_clergy} the same week, as you were bound to. He thanked you. He said it would be handled. It has been handled: the man is gone, the letter says nothing, and the woman's son is twenty-six and has not been inside a church in ten years. There will be no announcement, no name, no explanation to the people who sat in those pews. It is, you are told, the way it is done now, which is better than the way it was done. You believe that it is better. You also lay awake on Sunday night and found that the thing you had given your life to had a face you had not seen before, and that it was the face of an institution protecting itself first, and that you are in it, wearing its collar, and were thanked.
events.flavorPrompt: Institutional doubt: a brother priest quietly removed after an allegation the player himself carried to the chancery, and a parish told nothing. The player is never the accused. No melodrama; the wrong is in the silence.

choices.label: Say from the ambo, at {parish}, that the people of that parish were owed the truth
choices.outcome: You do not name the man or the parish. You say that the Church has learned to remove and has not yet learned to tell, and that a people asked to pray for personal reasons deserve to know what they are praying about. It is in the diocesan paper's inbox by Monday. {@vicar_for_clergy} calls, not angry, tired. {@pastor} says nothing, which is loud. You said it. It is on the record now, and so are you.

choices.label: Write to {@bishop}, privately, and say what you think the letter should have said
choices.outcome: It is two pages, and it is careful, and it does not accuse anyone of anything except of saying too little. His reply comes on his own stationery and is courteous and says that he shares your concern and that these matters are constrained in ways he cannot always explain. It is not nothing. You have said it to the man who could change it, and he has told you, politely, that he will not, and you know where you stand.

choices.label: Go back to the woman and her son, and be the one person in the Church who tells them what happened
choices.outcome: She had already worked it out from the letter. Her son will not see you, and then, a month later, does, in a diner, for twenty minutes, and says nothing you can repeat and does not need to. You have told nobody what the diocese would not, and you have not fixed anything, and you have stood where you could stand. {@vicar_for_clergy} would call it inappropriate contact if he knew. He does not.

choices.label: Decide that you cannot wear the collar of an institution that does this, and go
choices.outcome: You take a year to be sure, because you owe it that. In the year nothing changes. You tell {@bishop} in his office, and you tell him why, and he does not defend it, which is the nearest to an admission you will get. You leave the collar on the desk. It is the hardest thing you have done and it is, you are certain, the honest one.

effects.value: He left the priesthood after a brother priest was removed in silence and a parish told nothing, having carried the allegation to the chancery himself. He did not leave the Church. He left its clergy, and said publicly why, once, and then declined every invitation to say it again. The woman's son came to the small farewell gathering, and stood at the back.

events.title: A house with a light on
events.body: There is no crisis. You believe what you believed, you have not fallen in love, you are not drinking, the parish is fine and {@pastor} is no worse than usual. It is a Saturday in autumn and you have done a wedding at two and a baptism at four and you are driving back to the rectory through a neighborhood of ordinary houses, and one of them has a light on in the kitchen and a man at the sink and a child at the table, and you slow down, and you do not know why you slowed down. That is a lie. You know exactly why. You have been a good priest for some years and you would like, for one evening, to be nobody's Father: to come home to someone who did not need anything from you, to have a Saturday that was not somebody else's wedding, to be a man in a kitchen. It is not a temptation. It is a grief, and it is for a life you gave away on purpose and would give away again, probably, if asked, and nobody is asking; the giving was done once, in a cathedral, and it goes on being done every Saturday at dusk in a car. You turn in at the rectory. The light is off.
events.flavorPrompt: The quiet doubt: not belief, not scandal, the plain wanting of an ordinary life. Autumn, a car, a lit kitchen window. Grief, not temptation. Write it with respect.

choices.label: Say it aloud to someone who will not try to fix it
choices.outcome: You say it to an old priest you trust, and he does not offer you consolation or the literature of consolation. He says that he has slowed down at that window every autumn for forty years and that it never stopped and that he would not, now, have it otherwise, because a man who did not want the other life had not given anything. You are not sure that is true. It is the truest thing anyone has said to you about it.

choices.label: Drive faster past that street from now on
choices.outcome: You take a different road home on Saturdays. It is a small thing, and it works, and you know from every other man you have watched do it that what is not looked at does not go away but goes underneath, and comes up in other forms: an edge in the confessional, an impatience with couples, a certain way of preaching about sacrifice that the parish will hear before you do. For now, it is a different road.

choices.label: Ask {@bishop} for a leave of absence, and say plainly why
choices.outcome: He hears you out and says no, not yet, because a year away is where most men who go do not come back from, and he would rather you found out here. He offers a change of assignment instead, which is not what you asked for and is an answer. It is in your file now, honestly stated: that you asked. The chancery does not forget that a man asked. Neither, you find, do you.

choices.label: Go home to a kitchen of your own
choices.outcome: It takes the better part of a year, done properly: the conversation with {@bishop}, the leave, the petition to Rome, the last Mass, which you do not announce as the last. Nobody is scandalized, because there is nothing to be scandalized by. You were a good priest who wanted the other life more, and you were honest enough to say so before it made you a worse one.

effects.value: He left the priesthood a few years into parish ministry, not over doubt or scandal but because he wanted an ordinary life and would not pretend otherwise. He did it properly: a leave, a petition, a dispensation. He married later, and had the kitchen, and went to Mass on Sundays at a parish where the pastor knew, and never said.

events.title: A year since
events.body: The card comes in the ordinary mail, in {@spiritual_director}'s handwriting, which has gotten smaller. It says that he hopes the parish is well and that he is still at the same place on Wednesdays, and nothing else, because he would not say more. You look at the calendar and count and it has been thirteen months. You did not decide to stop. You decided, each month, that this month was not the month, because the drive is an hour and a half each way and the Wednesdays are full and because, if you are honest, a man who has stopped going to direction does not want to say, in direction, that he has stopped going to direction. In the seminary it was required and you resented it slightly and went. Now it is only expected, by the Church in general and nobody in particular, and the general expectation has turned out to be no expectation at all. You know what a priest without a director becomes, because you have watched several of them at deanery meetings. The card is on the desk. He is still at the same place on Wednesdays.
events.flavorPrompt: A quiet card from the old spiritual director, thirteen months since the last visit. The lapse is inertia, not rebellion. Undramatic, honest.

choices.label: Mean to, again, and put the card in the drawer
choices.outcome: You will go next month. You write it on the calendar, and next month it is Lent, and the month after that there is the school's confirmation, and the card stays in the drawer with the other things you mean to do. He does not write again. He is not the kind to. You are a priest who had a director once, and knows he should have one, and this is how the knowing goes.

choices.label: Drive out on Wednesday, and tell him it has been thirteen months
choices.outcome: He does not remark on the thirteen months. He asks what the year has been, and you find that you cannot say it in less than the whole hour, and that some of it you had not known until you heard yourself say it. On the drive home the road is the same road and the parish is the same parish and you have put down something you had not noticed you were carrying. You write the next date in before you forget.

choices.label: Write and thank him, and find someone twenty minutes away
choices.outcome: You write him a real letter, and he writes back that this is the right thing and that he had hoped you would do it. The new man is a retired pastor in the next deanery with a good chair and a dog, and he is not the same, and he is there. It is a lesser thing than what you had. It is a thing you will actually do, which the greater thing had stopped being.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} whom he sees, and whether he still does
choices.outcome: He is embarrassed to be asked and then, unexpectedly, glad. He has not seen anyone in years, he says, and names a monk at the abbey two hours off whom he saw once and liked. You go together, the next month, in his car, and do not talk about it on the way, and do on the way back. It is the closest the two of you have been. You keep going, and mostly he does too.

events.title: The retreat
events.body: The law asks that a priest make a retreat regularly, and {diocese} reads regularly as annually and provides one: five days in June at the retreat house by the lake, a preacher brought in from another diocese, conferences at ten and three, the rooms with the thin mattresses, the presbyterate in polo shirts. It is fine. It is also, everyone knows, the week the diocese's priests catch up on each other, and the conferences are well attended and the evenings are better attended, and a man can come back rested without having prayed much. The alternatives are yours to arrange: a Trappist house four hours north that takes priests in silence, a house on the shore that three of your class rent every year and call a retreat with a straight face, or the option the chancery's form politely allows, which is to write in the date and the place of a private retreat and have no one check. {@pastor} says he stopped going to the diocesan one in the nineties and will cover the parish whichever week you choose. He does not say what he does instead.
events.flavorPrompt: The annual priests' retreat as a fact of diocesan life: half prayer, half reunion. The choice is what kind of week the player wants and what it costs the parish.

choices.label: Go to the diocesan retreat by the lake
choices.outcome: The preacher is competent and the lake is the lake. You pray more than you expected in the mornings and less than you meant in the evenings, which go late on the porch with men you had only known by name. You come back knowing the diocese better and yourself about the same, and {@pastor} has managed the week without incident and says so slightly pointedly.

choices.label: Book the Trappist house, in silence, for a week
choices.outcome: Nobody speaks to you for six days except the guestmaster, once, about the hot water. You sleep, and then you pray, and then, about Thursday, something in you that had been talking without pause for a year stops. You come back to a parish that got on without you and a presbyterate that missed the chance to look you over. It was the real thing. It was also a week the diocese did not see you.

choices.label: Take the house on the shore with {@closest_classmate} and the others
choices.outcome: You say Mass together each morning at the kitchen table, which counts for something, and the rest is fishing and cooking and the kind of talk about the diocese that cannot be had anywhere the diocese is listening. It is the best week of the year. You come back closer to the men you will spend forty years with and no closer to God than you left, and you are honest enough to know which of those the form was asking about.

choices.label: Write a date on the form, and use the week for the parish
choices.outcome: The form goes in with a plausible place and a plausible week, and the week itself goes to the things that were waiting: the school, the hospital list, the couples. The parish is better for it. Nobody checks; nobody ever checks. You have told the chancery a small untruth on paper and told the Church in general that its expectation was not, this year, your priority, and both of those are true facts about you now.

events.title: Monday
events.body: Monday is your day off. It says so on the parish website under Staff, and {@secretary} defends it against the parish with the ferocity of a woman who has watched four vicars not take it. What actually happens on Monday is that you sleep until eight, which feels like a sin, and by nine the phone has rung twice, and one of the calls is a family that has lost someone over the weekend and needs to see a priest today and {@pastor} does not do that anymore. By eleven you are in the office in a sweater instead of the collar, which is the only difference between Monday and Tuesday. You know the argument for the day off. You made it, once, in a seminary conference on the human pillar, with some feeling. You also know that the parish does not have a day off, that the funeral home does not, and that the vicar who takes his Monday is the vicar the parish will describe, kindly, as a little precious. This Monday is like the others. The sweater is on the chair. The phone is on the desk, and it is, at eight-fifteen, still quiet.
events.flavorPrompt: The day off that never gets taken. Domestic, wry, specific. The trade-off is real: the parish rewards the man who never stops and quietly wears him out.

choices.label: Put the sweater on and go down to the office
choices.outcome: The family is seen. The bulletin gets done. {@secretary} says nothing and closes her door a little harder than usual. The parish, which sees everything, notes that the young priest is always there, and approves, and asks a little more of him next week, because he is always there. You did not take Monday. You have not taken Monday in some time, and you have stopped counting, which is the part that would have worried the man who gave the conference.

choices.label: Turn the phone off, drive somewhere, and be nobody's Father until dark
choices.outcome: You drive an hour to a town where no one knows you and eat lunch in a diner and walk by a river and read a novel on a bench. The family is seen by {@pastor}, who is not pleased, and is seen. You come back at dusk not holy, only rested, which turns out to have been the point. The parish will call it precious. The parish will also, next year, have a priest who is still there.

choices.label: Give Monday to the diocesan committee that asked for you
choices.outcome: The committee meets on Mondays because Mondays are when priests are free, which tells you what the chancery thinks a day off is. You are good in the room, and the vicar general notices, and your name goes on the list of men who can be asked. It is the beginning of something and the parish does not see it, and the day off is now a day on somewhere else, which is how it starts for the useful ones.

events.title: The body
events.body: The cassock hides it, which is one of the arguments for the cassock. Two years of funeral lunches and the housekeeper's cooking and the box of doughnuts that appears in the sacristy every Sunday from a parishioner who loves you, and the clerical shirt that fit at ordination now does not, and you have caught yourself on the stairs to the choir loft breathing in a way that a man your age should not. Priests are not, as a class, healthy. You have seen the presbyterate at the chrism Mass; you have seen what fifty looks like in a man who has eaten at wakes for twenty-five years and has nobody at home to notice. There is a gym in town where two of the deacons go. There is a road behind the cemetery where a man could run at six, before the seven o'clock Mass, and be seen by no one but the groundskeeper. There is the alternative, which is to decide that the body is the last thing on a long list and let it go quietly the way most of them do. {@pastor} weighs what he weighs and has views about priests who jog.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest noticing his body going the way of the presbyterate's. Dry, physical, specific. The pastor disapproves of jogging.

choices.label: Run the cemetery road at six, before Mass
choices.outcome: The first week is humiliating and the groundskeeper pretends not to see. By the second month you are up before the alarm, and the seven o'clock Mass is said by a man who is awake, and the shirt fits again by Advent. {@pastor} refers to it as your hobby. The parish, which sees you on the road, decides it likes a priest who runs, and a few of the men join you on Saturdays, which was not the plan and is not unwelcome.

choices.label: Join the gym in town with the deacons
choices.outcome: The gym is a public place, and a priest in a public place is on duty whether he likes it or not. You are asked about annulments on the treadmill. You are asked to bless a man's shoulder. You are also seen, three mornings a week, being an ordinary man doing an ordinary thing, and it does more for the parish's view of the clergy than a year of homilies. The deacons are good company and know everything about everyone.

choices.label: Let it go. There are more important things, and the cassock hides it.
choices.outcome: The shirt is replaced by a larger shirt. The stairs to the loft become a thing you plan for. It is, in the end, what most of them do, and it is not a sin and the parish does not mind; the parish rather likes a priest who looks like he eats what they bring him. You will pay for it in twenty years, in the way the presbyterate pays, and you have decided, without quite deciding, that twenty years is someone else's problem.

events.title: In the sacristy, after
events.body: It happens after the ten-thirty, in the sacristy, with the vestments half off: a pressure in the chest that is not pain exactly, and a greyness at the edge of the room, and the server asking if you are all right in a voice that tells you what you look like. You sit down on the vesting bench. It passes in four minutes. You say you are fine and you finish unvesting and you go to the parish hall for the coffee and shake the hands, and nobody knows except the server, who is fourteen and will tell his mother. You have no doctor in this town. You have the diocesan health plan and a card in a drawer and the number of a parishioner who is a cardiologist and who said, at a dinner, to call him if you ever needed anything, in the way people say it. {@pastor} had something like this at forty-five and did nothing and is still here, which he would offer as evidence. It is Sunday afternoon. The greyness is gone. There is a wake at four and the thing in your chest has been, for an hour now, perfectly quiet, which is either good news or the kind of quiet a man learns to fear.
events.flavorPrompt: A cardiac scare in the sacristy after Mass, minimized and carried alone. Concrete and unmelodramatic. The temptation is to do what the presbyterate does, which is nothing.

choices.label: See a doctor this week, and tell {@pastor} why you need the Thursday
choices.outcome: The doctor uses a word you did not expect, which is arrhythmia, and another, which is stress, and refers you on, and it is not nothing and it is not the end. {@pastor} covers Thursday and asks, when you get back, how you are, and means it; he is not as indifferent as he plays. The parish learns you went to a doctor and decides you are human, which you had not known was in doubt.

choices.label: See a doctor two towns over, on your day off, and tell no one
choices.outcome: The doctor two towns over knows nothing about you and says the same two words, arrhythmia and stress, and gives you a prescription and a follow-up. You fill the prescription at a pharmacy where no one knows you either. It is handled. It is handled the way a priest handles things, alone, and the pattern is now set that your body is a private matter in a life that has almost no other private matters, and that will hold until it does not.

choices.label: Call the parishioner who said to call, and let him be a parishioner
choices.outcome: He sees you the next morning in his office before his first appointment, and does the tests himself, and is gentle and precise and tells you what it is and what to do, and then says, at the door, that it was a privilege to be asked. You have let a parishioner do something for you. It is a thing priests are bad at and parishes are hungry for, and the parish, which learns everything, learns this too.

choices.label: Do what {@pastor} did. Say the wake at four.
choices.outcome: You say the wake, and the Monday funeral, and it does not happen again that month, and by Advent you have nearly stopped listening for it. You have joined the presbyterate's oldest tradition, which is to treat the body as a thing that belongs to the parish and does not get a say. It is not courage. It is a bet, and the presbyterate's record on the bet is in the necrology, which you read every November.

effects.value: a cardiac episode after Mass, never followed up

events.title: The second call
events.body: The first call was a neighbor, in the spring: {@mother} had left the stove on, and it was nothing, and you drove down on your Monday and it was nothing. The second call is the neighbor again, and this time it is the car, which she drove to the church she has driven to for fifty years and could not find the way home from, and the police brought her back and were kind. You drive down. She is embarrassed and angry and perfectly lucid about the anger and less so about the car, and the house has the look houses get when the person in them has begun to lose track: the mail in stacks, the same three groceries. She will not hear of anything. She has a priest for a son and a parish of her own and the neighbor, and she will be fine, and she says this while looking for her glasses, which are on her head. You are a parochial vicar three hours away with a Sunday schedule and no money and a pastor who has already told you, in another context, that a priest's family is not the parish's problem. She is your mother. There is no one else, or no one else who will.
events.flavorPrompt: The mother's decline begins: a lost drive home, a house going wrong. The son is a priest three hours away with no money and a full Sunday. Tender, unsentimental, practical.

choices.label: Find her a place near {parish}, and do the moving yourself
choices.outcome: It takes a month of Mondays and every favor you have: a senior apartment four blocks from the church, the parish's van for the boxes, {@secretary}'s cousin who knows the manager. She hates it and then does not. She comes to your Mass and sits in the third pew and tells the women around her which parts you got from her. You see her every day, for ten minutes, and the ten minutes are now the fixed point your week is built around.

choices.label: Leave her where she is, and drive down every Monday for as long as it takes
choices.outcome: Three hours down, the afternoon with her, three hours back in the dark, every week. She stays in her house and her parish, which is what she wanted, and the neighbor calls you when the neighbor needs to, which is more often each month. Monday is gone, entirely, and so is much of Tuesday. {@pastor} says nothing, which is his way of saying it. You are doing the thing a son does. You are doing it at the edge of what a vicar can.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} for the empty room upstairs
choices.outcome: You expect a no and get a long silence and then a yes, on conditions: she eats with the two of you, she does not answer the rectory phone, and she is your responsibility. She moves in with two suitcases and a photograph of your father and takes over the kitchen within the week. {@pastor} pretends to mind. The parish is charmed and the presbyterate is amused, and the diocese, which does not have a rule about this, now has a case.

choices.label: Tell her it has to be someone else, and mean it
choices.outcome: You say it in her kitchen: that you are a priest, that you have a parish, that there are other people whose turn this is. She agrees too quickly. You drive back in daylight for once. The other people take it up, unevenly, with the resentment of people who have watched the priest in the family be excused from things for years. You have kept the parish whole. You will wonder, on Mondays, for a long time.

events.title: The funeral you have to preach
events.body: {@father} died on a Tuesday, in the hospital, with you there, which is more than most sons get and which you will be grateful for later. Now it is Wednesday and the funeral director, who knows you are a priest and is therefore both deferential and efficient, has asked the question everyone has been careful not to: who is going to preach. The pastor of the home parish has offered, decently, and has also said, in the same breath, that of course if you would rather. Your family assumes it will be you. The parish where he is to be buried assumes it. You have preached perhaps two hundred funerals for other people's fathers and you know how to do it in your sleep, and you know, sitting at the kitchen table with the readings the family wants, that the thing you know how to do is precisely what you cannot do here. You cannot say the things you say. You would have to say the true things, about him, and some of the true things are not the kind you say from an ambo, and the family is in the front row, and you are the priest and you are the son and the Church has no rite for being both at once.
events.flavorPrompt: The player's father has died and the family expects the priest-son to preach. Grief, craft, and the impossibility of using the usual funeral voice on your own father. Exact about the rite.

choices.label: Preach it. Say the true things, in the voice you use for other people's fathers.
choices.outcome: You get through it, which is what everyone says afterward, and it is not what you did. You said who he was, including the parts that were hard, in the register you have learned for strangers, and it held, and at the commendation your voice went and came back. The parish of your childhood has never heard a homily like it. Your family will quote it for years. You will not remember most of it.

effects.value: dead

choices.label: Concelebrate, and let the home pastor preach, and sit with your family for the homily
choices.outcome: You vest and stand at the altar and let another man say the words, and at the homily you go down and sit in the front pew in a chasuble and sit with the people who knew him longest. The homily is fine. It is about a man the preacher barely knew and it is fine. You were the son for twelve minutes and the priest for the rest, and it was the right division, and it cost you the one thing everyone expected.

effects.value: dead

choices.label: Preach it, and say the thing between the two of you that was never said
choices.outcome: You say from the ambo that he did not want you to be a priest, and why, and that he was not wrong about the cost, and that he came to the ordination anyway and sat in the back. The family goes still. The home pastor looks at the floor. It was true, and he is dead, and you have told a church full of people the one thing he would have wanted kept, and you are not sure, driving back, whether it was for him or for you.

effects.value: dead

events.title: Six thousand
events.body: {@sibling} calls on a weeknight, which is unusual, and talks about nothing for ten minutes, which is the tell, and then says it: six thousand dollars, by the fifteenth, or the truck goes, and without the truck there is no work, and there is a child. It is not the first time. It is the first time since ordination, and the number is bigger, and the voice on the phone has the particular flatness of a person who has run out of people to ask and has arrived at the priest. A parochial vicar in {diocese} is paid what he is paid, which is enough for a man with no rent and no family, and you have some of it, less than six, in an account you have not looked at in months. There is also, and you dislike that you have thought of it, the parish: the discretionary fund {@pastor} lets you draw on for the poor, which your family arguably is, and the petty cash, which nobody counts. {@sibling} does not know about either. The fifteenth is nine days away. The child's name is said on the phone twice, which was not an accident.
events.flavorPrompt: A sibling asks the priest in the family for money he does not really have. The parish's cash is right there. Pressure, love, and the tempting wrong option. Keep the sibling's gender unstated.

choices.label: Send what you have, all of it, and say nothing about the rest
choices.outcome: It is four thousand and change, and it goes by wire on a Thursday, and {@sibling} cries on the phone and then, in the same call, asks whether the parish might help with the rest, and you say no in a voice you did not know you had. The truck stays. The account is empty. You are the priest in the family and this is, apparently, what the priest in the family is for, and you find that you do not mind as much as you should.

choices.label: Say no. You are not a bank, and it is not the first time.
choices.outcome: You say it as kindly as it can be said, which is not very. {@sibling} does not argue, which is worse than arguing. The truck goes on the sixteenth. There is a long silence from that quarter that lasts through Christmas, and your mother, or whoever is left, takes a side, and it is not yours. You kept your money and the principle. The principle was sound, and you will be a long time finding out what it cost.

choices.label: Take it from the discretionary fund, as a loan, and pay it back over the year
choices.outcome: You write it in the ledger as assistance to a family in need, which is not false. {@sibling} gets six thousand and the truck stays. You pay it back, mostly, over fourteen months, and nobody asks, because nobody looks. It is the first time you have used the parish's money for your own family, and you told yourself it was a loan, and the ledger says otherwise, and the ledger is what a chancery reads.

effects.value: used the parish discretionary fund to cover a family debt, recorded as assistance

choices.label: Drive down with a legal pad and go through every number together
choices.outcome: It takes a Monday and most of the night. The truck loan can be refinanced; the other debt, the one that was not mentioned on the phone, cannot, but can be negotiated, and you make the calls yourself in a voice that has learned to talk to banks. You send two thousand toward the gap. {@sibling} is humiliated and then, by the end, not. The truck stays. So does the legal pad, on the fridge, with the plan on it.

events.title: A baptism in the family
events.body: The baby is six weeks old and {@sibling} wants the baptism done by you, at {parish} or at home, whichever is easier, and would like it before the grandmother's birthday, which is a real reason and also the whole reason. {@sibling} has not been inside a church since your ordination. The baby's other parent is not Catholic and is politely indifferent. The godparents proposed are a college roommate and a cousin who is, you happen to know, not confirmed. None of this is unusual; you do four of these a month for strangers and you know the questions and the pastoral latitude and the line in the canon about a founded hope that the child will be raised in the faith, and you know how generously most priests read it, and why. What is unusual is that it is your family, that the grandmother is your mother or your aunt, that the baby has your surname or nearly, and that {@sibling} is asking you not as a priest but as a brother, and has no idea that there is a difference, and would be wounded to learn it. The photograph is already planned: you in the stole, the baby in the family gown, the grandmother beside the font.
events.flavorPrompt: A sibling wants the priest in the family to baptize a baby, for the grandmother, with no intention of practicing. Canon 868's founded hope, read generously or not. Family warmth against pastoral honesty. Keep the sibling's gender unstated.

choices.label: Do it at {parish}, on a Sunday, with the whole family in the front pews
choices.outcome: The family fills three pews and does not know when to sit and stand and does not care. You baptize the child in the gown your mother was baptized in, and the grandmother weeps at the font, and {@pastor} shakes every hand at the door. Whether the child is raised in anything is a question you have set aside, the way most priests do, for love. The photograph is on the fridge in two houses by Tuesday.

choices.label: Say yes, and ask for one evening first, the two of you, about what the promises mean
choices.outcome: You drive down and sit in the kitchen with the baby asleep and say what the parents will be asked to promise and what it would mean to mean it. {@sibling} is uncomfortable and honest and says, eventually, that it is for the grandmother, and you say that you know, and that you will do it anyway, and that you are asking for one Sunday a month afterward. It is not a promise. It is the beginning of one, and you have at least made the question real.

choices.label: Say that the law asks for a founded hope, and that you do not yet have one, and ask to wait
choices.outcome: You say it as gently as a hard thing can be said and {@sibling} hears only the no. The grandmother's birthday passes without the photograph. A priest at the home parish does it the following spring, without the questions, and you are not invited. You were right in law and possibly in fact, and you have lost something in your family that a founded hope will be a long time restoring, and you would do it again, and you are not sure that is to your credit.

events.title: The fourth pew on the left
events.body: She is in the fourth pew on the left at the ten-thirty, with a husband and a boy of about four, and she has been there, you work out afterward, for three Sundays, and you did not see her because you do not look at the fourth pew on the left, because nobody does. This Sunday you looked. The husband is pleasant-looking and sang. The boy dropped a toy. She did not come up for Communion in your line; she went to {@pastor}'s, which was either an accident or the most careful thing anyone has done in that church. She is registered. {@secretary} says so, when you ask a question you frame as being about a family you did not recognize: they moved into the subdivision in August, they are in the young families' group, the husband has volunteered for the fish fry. She knows what you are. She chose this parish anyway, or the husband did, or the subdivision did. You were going to marry her once. You told the diocese so, at application, in a paragraph you have never reread. She is in your parish now, and her son will be in the school, and you will be the priest who hears the family's confessions, unless you are not.
events.flavorPrompt: The woman the player nearly married is now a registered parishioner with a husband and child. Restraint, precision, no melodrama. The question is how to be her priest.

choices.label: Greet them at the door next Sunday, by name, like any family
choices.outcome: You shake the husband's hand and learn his name and ask the boy about the toy. She says Father with a straight face and you say her name with one. It takes eleven seconds, like the promise of obedience did, and it is done, and it is the hardest eleven seconds of the year. The parish sees a priest greeting a new family. Only two people in the narthex know what they saw, and both of them have decided to be adults.

choices.label: Trade the ten-thirty with {@pastor} and give no reason
choices.outcome: {@pastor} takes the trade, curious, and you take the eight, which is older and quieter. It works, in that you do not see her, and it does not work, in that the parish is one parish and the school is one school and the fish fry has one line. You have organized your Sundays around a woman in the fourth pew, which is, you notice, precisely the thing you would have had to do if you had married her.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} who she is, so that he has heard it from you
choices.outcome: You tell him after Mass in the sacristy, in three sentences, and he listens and says only that he is glad you told him and that he will take the family's sacramental prep. He does not make it more than it is. Nobody in {parish} will ever hear of it from him. You have put the one fact that could be used against you into the hands of the one man who could use it, and he has, so far, been the right man.

choices.label: Ask her to coffee, once, to say the things that were never said
choices.outcome: It is a chain place off the highway and it is an hour and it is the most honest hour you have had with anyone in years. She says she is happy, and is. You say you are, and mostly are. Nothing is renewed and nothing is regretted aloud. But a parishioner from the young families' group is in the corner booth, and sees the collar and the woman and the hour, and does not know what it was, and will describe it.

effects.value: seen alone at length with a married parishioner he was once engaged to

events.title: In their own hand
events.body: The envelope is not from the mother. The handwriting is younger and the return address is a college town, and the letter inside is two pages, careful, and begins by saying that its writer has known for some years and has waited until eighteen because that seemed fair, and would like to meet you, once, if you are willing, and will understand if you are not. It does not accuse you of anything. It does not ask for anything except an hour. It says, near the end, that the writer is not looking for a father and has one, and is looking for the answer to a question that cannot be asked of anyone else, and that the question is not what you think. You have known this day was somewhere on the calendar since the year before you entered, when you and the mother agreed the terms, and you have imagined it as a confrontation, and it is not that. It is a courteous request from an adult you have never met who shares your face, and who has been fair to you, and who has your address, and the diocese's, and a life of their own. The letter is dated a week ago. You read it four times at the desk with the door shut.
events.flavorPrompt: The player's child, born before seminary and never raised by him, turns eighteen and writes asking to meet once. Write with great care: the child is an adult, fair, and owed the truth. No melodrama, no self-pity. Keep the child's gender unstated.

choices.label: Tell {@vicar_for_clergy} and {@pastor} first, and then go, in daylight, as who you are
choices.outcome: {@vicar_for_clergy} already had the file and says only that he is glad you told him before and not after. {@pastor} says nothing for a long moment and then that you should take the car. You meet in a café in the college town, two hours, and the question is about whether the leaving was because of them, and you answer it truthfully, which is no, and it is the most important sentence you will say that year. Nobody in {parish} knows. The diocese does, correctly.

choices.label: Go, on a Monday, and tell no one, and ask that it stay between you
choices.outcome: The hour is the same hour, in the same café, and the question is the same question, and the answer is the same true answer. What is different is the last five minutes, in which you ask a person who has been fair to you for eighteen years to keep a secret for your sake, and they agree, with a look you will remember. The diocese, which has the file, does not have this. You have made your child a party to your discretion.

effects.value: met his adult child in secret and asked them to keep it quiet

choices.label: Answer the letter with a letter: the whole truth, and no meeting
choices.outcome: It is six pages and it takes a week and it answers the question, and it says at the end that you will meet if they still want to after reading it, and leaves the choice there, where it belongs. The reply, a month later, is one page, and says thank you, and does not ask to meet, and does not close the door. You have told the truth on paper to the one person who was owed it, and you have not looked them in the face.

choices.label: Write back, kindly, that the agreement was the agreement, and that you cannot
choices.outcome: It is a short letter and a decent one and it is a no, and it was the terms, and the terms were agreed by two people who were not the person now asking. The reply does not come. You keep the letter in the drawer, and you say Mass the next morning, and the prayer for the faithful has a line about children, and you say it in the same voice as the rest. It is the last time this door will open from that side.

events.title: The photograph
events.body: The photograph is fifteen years old and you are in it, younger and thinner, with a sign and a look of certainty you no longer have the face for, being led away from a gate by a police officer who is, in the picture, more embarrassed than you. It was in a newspaper once. Now it is on a parish Facebook group, posted by a man from the finance council with the caption Is this our new Father, and under it, by Monday morning, are sixty comments, and {@secretary} has printed them out, which is how she expresses concern. The diocese knows about the arrest; it was in your file at application, and the vocation director said it was not disqualifying and asked whether you were still that kind of person, and you said something careful. Half the comments are delighted. Half are not. A woman from the diocesan paper has left a message asking for a quote, cheerfully. {@pastor} has read the printout and put it on your desk with no note, which is either trust or a test. You believed in the thing on the sign then. You have not, in fact, stopped. What has changed is that you now wear a collar, and the collar is not yours alone.
events.flavorPrompt: An old protest arrest photograph surfaces on a parish social media group. The player's past conviction, now attached to the collar. The chancery watches; both blocs watch.

choices.label: Give the paper the quote: yes, that was you, and you would stand there again
choices.outcome: The quote runs on page three under the photograph, and it is a good quote, and the parish's two halves each decide they were right about you. The chancery notes that the young vicar is now a name. Invitations arrive from people who want a priest at a gate. {@pastor} says, at dinner, that he hopes you enjoy committees, because that is where they send men who say things in the paper, and then adds that he does not disagree with you.

choices.label: Decline the quote, and write to {@bishop} to say what you believe and that you will not preach it
choices.outcome: The letter says that the photograph is accurate, that the conviction behind it has not changed, and that you understand the difference between what a man believes and what a priest says from the ambo, and intend to keep it. {@bishop} writes back one line thanking you for the clarity. The Facebook thread dies of its own weight. The chancery has a file that says exactly who you are, which is either the safest or the most dangerous thing a file can say.

choices.label: Tell the paper it was a long time ago and you were young
choices.outcome: It is what they wanted to hear and the thread cools. The finance council man is satisfied. The half of the parish that was delighted is quieter now, and looks at you differently, and the man you were in the photograph would not have crossed the street to speak to the man who gave that quote. You did not lie. You said the thing that ends conversations, and the photograph still exists, and so does the conviction, and both of them keep.

effects.value: publicly distanced himself from a conviction he still holds

choices.label: Say nothing to the paper, and preach on Sunday about what the sign said, without the sign
choices.outcome: The homily does not mention the photograph or the gate or the arrest. It is about the thing the sign was about, from the Gospel, in a voice that is not a protest voice, and it is the best homily you have preached in {parish}, and both halves of the parish come out unsure which half won. The paper does not get its quote. The chancery gets a recording, from someone, and listens to it, and finds nothing to object to, and remembers it.

events.title: A routine evaluation
events.body: The letter from {@vicar_for_clergy}'s office is form-printed and says that {diocese}, following a review, now asks every priest under ten years ordained to complete a psychological evaluation before any change of assignment, and that yours is scheduled, and that it is routine. It is routine. It was brought in after a bad year for the diocese that everyone knows about and no one names, and it is being applied to every young priest without exception, and the men are grumbling about it at deanery meetings in the way men grumble about a thing they are secretly relieved is not aimed at them. It is not aimed at you. It will nonetheless ask, in the intake questionnaire, whether you have ever been hospitalized for a psychiatric condition, and whether you have ever been prescribed medication for one, and whether there has been a period in your life when you were unable to function, and you know the answers, and the diocese knows some of them, because they were disclosed at application in a paragraph the vocation director read with his glasses off. The evaluator is a layman with a practice in the city who does this for three dioceses. He will have the seminary file, or he will not. The questionnaire is due Friday.
events.flavorPrompt: A diocese-wide psychological evaluation, routine in name, that will ask about the player's breakdown before seminary. The temptation is to minimize; the file may already say it. Bureaucratic, precise.

choices.label: Answer every question in full, including the ones the file already answers
choices.outcome: The evaluator reads your answers and then reads the file and looks up and says that they match, which in his experience they often do not. The interview is long and not unkind. The report says what the seminary's said, that there was an episode, that it was treated, that it has not recurred, and adds a line about the honesty of the subject that {@vicar_for_clergy} underlines. You have been examined and found to be the man you said you were.

choices.label: Answer the questions narrowly, and let the file say what it says
choices.outcome: You answer the hospitalization question with a technicality and the medication question with a date range that is accurate and short. The evaluator has the file, as it turns out, and notices, and does not say so in the room. The report is clean. There is a sentence in it about a tendency to underreport that will mean nothing to anyone who is not looking for it, and the diocese, after its bad year, has learned to look.

effects.value: minimized a documented psychiatric history on a diocesan evaluation

choices.label: Write to {@vicar_for_clergy} first and ask that the seminary's evaluation be forwarded, so no one has to guess
choices.outcome: It is a two-paragraph letter and it does the diocese's work for it, which the diocese appreciates more than it should. The evaluator arrives with the whole file and the interview is half as long. {@vicar_for_clergy} mentions, later, that you were the only one of the year's cohort who thought to do that, and that it told him something. It told him you know how files work, which is a thing the chancery values in a man, and watches.

choices.label: Write to {@vicar_for_clergy} objecting to the policy, and comply under protest
choices.outcome: The letter says that a blanket evaluation of the young because of the sins of the old is a policy that punishes the wrong men, and that you will complete it because you were asked, and that you want the objection in the file beside the result. It goes in the file. The result is clean and honest. The presbyterate, which hears about the letter, is quietly grateful. The chancery is not, and the chancery is who reads the file.

events.title: Dinner
events.body: {@closest_classmate} calls to say he is leaving, and that he wanted you to hear it from him before the presbyterate's telephone got to it, and that he would like to have dinner. He is not asking permission and he is not asking to be talked out of it. He has been to {@bishop}. The leave is granted; the petition to Rome will follow; there is, he says without saying it, someone, and there has been for a while, and he is not sorry about that part. He says the restaurant and the day. Between the call and the day the telephone does its work, and the presbyterate has an opinion, and the opinion is the usual one, which is grief dressed as disapproval, and one or two of the older men say the thing about weak vocations, and one of the younger ones says he is a coward for not leaving sooner. He was the man who drove you back from the seminary the night your father called. He was the man you called at nine. He will not be a priest by Easter, and he has asked you to dinner, and everyone in {diocese} will know whether you went.
events.flavorPrompt: The player's closest classmate is leaving the priesthood, properly, for someone. He asks for dinner. The presbyterate watches. Friendship against the tribe; no contempt for either side.

choices.label: Go, and listen, and tell him you will be at whatever comes next
choices.outcome: He talks for two hours and you let him, and at the end you say that you will come to the wedding, if there is one, in a suit, and he puts his face in his hands for a moment. It is around the diocese within the week. Two older men stop returning your nods at the chrism Mass. He calls, afterward, less, and then more, and he is, in the end, the one friend you have who is not a priest and knows exactly what one is.

effects.value: left

choices.label: Go, and tell him what you think, which is that he promised
choices.outcome: You say it over the bread: that he knelt in a cathedral and put his hands between a bishop's hands and that this is a promise and not a preference. He does not argue back. He says he knows, and that he is breaking it, and that he wanted you to say it because nobody else would say it to his face. You part as friends, of a kind. The presbyterate hears that you went and what you said, and approves of both, and you are not sure it should.

effects.value: left

choices.label: Go, and tell him that you have stood at the same door
choices.outcome: You had not planned to say it and you say it, that there have been nights, and a window with a light on, and that you are still here and do not know entirely why. He looks at you for a long time and says that he had wondered, and that it does not make him think less of you, and that he hopes it does not make you think less of him. It is the truest conversation of your priesthood, and it is with a man leaving it.

effects.value: left

choices.label: Write instead. Say you cannot, and that you will pray for him.
choices.outcome: The letter is honest and it is a letter, and he does not answer it, and you understand why. The presbyterate approves, in the way it approves of things it would not have had the stomach for itself. You have kept faith with the tribe and not with the man who drove you home the night your father called. You will see him once more, years from now, in a hardware store, and you will both be kind, and it will not be the same.

effects.value: left

events.title: The anniversary
