events.body: It is in the ordo, with the other anniversaries of the diocese's priests, and {@secretary} has seen it, because she reads the ordo, and has asked whether you would like anything done. It is a weekday. There is the seven o'clock Mass, which you have, and a school Mass at nine, and the hospital list, and a couple at four. A year ago, or several, you lay on a cathedral floor while a litany was sung over you, and a bishop's hands were on your head, and your mother wept in the second row, and afterward there was a reception in a hall with a cake, and you gave your first blessing to the people who had made you, and it was the largest day of your life. Now it is a Wednesday in the same week, and the parish does not know, and would like to. The class has a group message about dinner on Saturday, at a steakhouse, which is what the class does. You could do nothing. It is possible that doing nothing is the truest observance: to say the seven o'clock as if it were any seven o'clock, because it is, and that was the point. It is also possible that a man who lets the day go by unmarked is telling himself something.
events.flavorPrompt: The anniversary of ordination on an ordinary weekday. The parish would like to celebrate; the class has a dinner; the priest could let it pass. Quiet, wry, sincere.

choices.label: Say the seven o'clock, and tell no one, and remember it
choices.outcome: You say the Mass to the fourteen people who come on a Wednesday, and at the memento you remember the floor and the hands and the second row, and you do not preach any longer than usual. Nobody knows. {@secretary} knows and says nothing, which is her gift. It was the right observance for a man who meant the ordinary thing to be the whole thing, and you go to the hospital at ten a little more than you were.

choices.label: Go to the steakhouse on Saturday with whoever is left of the class
choices.outcome: Fewer come each year, and the ones who come talk more. You learn who is in trouble and who is being watched and who has given up, and you say nothing about yourself that you would not say at a deanery meeting, and it is the best evening of the month. Driving home you do the arithmetic of how many of these dinners are left, and it is a large number, and it is a number.

choices.label: Let {@secretary} put it in the bulletin, and let the parish do what it does
choices.outcome: The parish does what it does, which is cake in the hall after the Sunday Mass and a card signed by the school, and a woman from the altar society who tells you that you are the best young priest they have had, in front of {@pastor}. It is warm, and it is real, and it is the beginning of the parish thinking of you as theirs, which is a thing the diocese will one day have to take away from them.

choices.label: Let it go by. It is a Wednesday.
choices.outcome: You do not remember it until the evening, when the group message reminds you, and you turn the phone over. The seven o'clock was a seven o'clock. You are not sure what it means that you forgot, and you decide not to find out, and you say Night Prayer, and it is, you notice, the first year that the day has not moved you, which is either maturity or the thing that looks like it.

events.title: The word
events.body: People have called you Father for a year, and it has been a title, a thing said at the door and in the office and by children who have been told to. You answer to it. Tonight it is the hospital, the fourth floor, a man of eighty-one whom you have never met, whose daughter called the rectory because the chaplain was off and someone had said there was a young priest at {parish} who would come. He is awake. He is not going to be awake much longer and knows it. You do the anointing, the oil on the forehead and the hands, the words, and it is a rite you have done thirty times and it goes as it goes. Then, as you are putting the oil stock away, he reaches over and takes your wrist, which is not strong, and says Father, and then says the thing he had been keeping for a priest for, it turns out, fifty years. And you hear the word. Not the title. The word, as a man says it who means that you are the one who can, and there is no one else in the room, and no one else who can, and you are twenty-nine, or thirty-eight, and you are.
events.flavorPrompt: The first time a dying stranger says Father and means it. Hospital room, anointing, an old man's confession. Restraint; the weight is in the word, not the prose.

choices.label: Stay until it is over
choices.outcome: It is four hours. The daughter goes for coffee and comes back and goes again. You say the prayers for the dying when it is time and you sit for the rest, and at some point after two he stops, and the daughter says Father, in the other way, the way that means thank you, and you drive home through an empty town and do not sleep and do not need to. Something has been settled that you did not know was open.

choices.label: Finish, bless them both, and go home to the seven o'clock
choices.outcome: You have a Mass in five hours and a school Mass after it, and you have done what a priest does and done it well, and you bless the daughter and leave your card. He dies before morning. You say the seven o'clock and it is a good Mass. You were what he needed and you were also a man with a schedule, and both were true, and the first one was, you understand now, the one that will be asked of you in the end.

choices.label: Stay, and in the morning tell {@pastor} what happened, because someone should know
choices.outcome: You tell him at breakfast, badly, because there is no good way, and he puts down the paper and listens to the whole of it, and when you are done he says that it happened to him in 1987 in a farmhouse and that he has never told anyone either. He does not say more. It is the first thing the two of you have had that was not the parish, and it is the thing, it turns out, that the parish is for.

events.title: The ten-thirty
events.body: You did not notice it happening. What you notice is the result, which is that the ten-thirty, which was {@pastor}'s Mass for twenty years and is now, by a rotation he set up himself, yours two Sundays in three, has grown. The ushers say so; the count in the sacristy says so. The eight o'clock, which is his, has not. People are coming to hear you preach. They say it at the door, without meaning anything by it, in front of him: we come to your Mass, Father. A family from the next parish has registered. The confession line on Saturday is longer on your side of the church, and {@secretary} has begun, without being asked, to route the hard calls to you. You are good at this. You are, you understand one Sunday at the door with a hand in yours and a face lit up over it, unusually good at this, and it is the first time in your life that a thing has come to you without being worked for, and the pleasure of it is enormous and not entirely clean. {@pastor} is at the other door. He has heard every word. He has been a priest for thirty-one years and no one is registering from the next parish for him.
events.flavorPrompt: The moment a young priest discovers he has a gift, at the door of the church, in front of the pastor who does not. Pleasure, envy, the beginning of a reputation. DESIGN 4.3: high charisma brings envy.

choices.label: Take it inside, say nothing, and go on doing the work
choices.outcome: You do not change anything. You preach as you preach and you do not look at the count. The parish goes on coming and {@pastor} goes on hearing it at the door, and you go on being careful in his presence in a way he notices and cannot object to. The chancery hears, from someone, that the vicar at {parish} can preach, and files it. You have a gift and have decided not to be seen holding it, which is a kind of holding.

choices.label: Lean into it: take the extra Mass, start the podcast, let the parish be yours
choices.outcome: Within a year the ten-thirty is standing room and the recording of it has listeners in three dioceses, and you are asked to preach at a neighboring parish's mission, and you are, at thirty or forty, a name. {@pastor} stops coming to the door. Two brother priests in the deanery have stopped returning your calls, and one has said the word showman where it would get back to you. The parish loves you. The parish is going to be very hard to leave.

choices.label: Give it to him, at the door and in the bulletin, and mean it
choices.outcome: You say, when the next hand lights up at you, that {@pastor} built this parish and you are only borrowing it, and you say it again at the parish council and in the bulletin column he lets you write. It is true enough. The parish believes it about half. {@pastor} believes it less and is grateful anyway, and something eases in the rectory. The gift is still yours. You have learned that it can be spent on someone else, which is the only thing a gift like that is for.

choices.label: Ask him to teach you the part you do not have, which is everything that is not the ten-thirty
choices.outcome: You say it at dinner: that you can preach and he can run a parish, and that you would like to learn the second thing from him. He is surprised, and then he is a teacher, which he has not been in years. The budget, the school board, the diocesan assessment, the boiler. It is not glamorous and the ten-thirty does not care. You have traded some of the pleasure for some of the craft, and he has stopped standing at the other door.

events.title: He's very smart
events.body: The wake is at the funeral home on the avenue, the family is large and loud and has been in {parish} for four generations, and you are there for the vigil prayers, which you say well. Afterward there is the part you are not good at: the hour in the room with the family, the coffee, the standing. You do not know what to say to the cousins. You say something about the readings. You say something about the deceased that you learned from the intake form. The widow is kind to you, which is how you know. On the way out you pass two of the men on the steps, and one of them, who did not see you, says of you to the other, well, he's very smart, in the tone in which a parish says everything it needs to about a priest. {@pastor}, who is not smart, would have stood in that room for an hour and said nothing of consequence and been loved. You have two degrees and a good mind and a bookshelf the parish has seen through the rectory window, and you have just learned that none of it is the thing, and that the thing is something {@pastor} has and you may not, and that the parish knew before you did.
events.flavorPrompt: The moment a bright young priest learns he is not good at the ordinary pastoral thing: a wake, a room full of family, nothing to say. DESIGN 4.3: high Knowledge reads as academic, not pastor. Honest, not self-pitying.

choices.label: Go to the next wake early, stand in the room, and say nothing until you can
choices.outcome: It takes a year and it does not come naturally and it comes. You learn to ask about the photographs. You learn that the silence is the work, and that the cousins do not want the readings, they want a priest who stays. The parish revises its opinion slowly and never entirely: he's very smart, they still say, and then, now, and he's good with the families. It cost you evenings you would rather have spent with the bookshelf, and you know exactly what it bought.

choices.label: Accept it, and put the mind where it is wanted: the adult classes, the diocesan paper, the seminary's guest lectures
choices.outcome: The classes fill, from three parishes. The column is read at the chancery. The seminary asks for a week in the spring. You are, within two years, the vicar the diocese calls when it wants something explained, and the wakes at {parish} are {@pastor}'s, and everyone is content, and the chancery has begun to say the sentence about you that ends in the word teaching, and you are not sure you will like the parish they think that sentence means.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to take you to the next one and let you watch
choices.outcome: He does not understand the question at first, because he has never thought of it as a thing that could be watched. Then he takes you. You stand behind him in a room on the avenue for an hour and see him do almost nothing, precisely, and afterward in the car he says the only thing he has ever said to you about the priesthood, which is that they do not want you to be interesting, they want you to be there. You write it down.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor}, plainly, that you are not sure you are built for this
choices.outcome: He listens and says that nobody is, and that half the men who look built for it are faking and the other half are not sure either, and that the parish will forgive a priest almost anything except not showing up. It is not reassurance. It is information. You go to the next wake anyway, and you are not good at it, and you are there, and the widow's kindness has a slightly different quality, and you take it.

events.title: Christmas afternoon
events.body: The last Mass ends at half past twelve and by one the church is empty and the smell of the pine and the candles is the only thing left of five Masses in eighteen hours. {@pastor} has gone to his sister's, as he does, and left a note and a plate. The housekeeper is off until the twenty-seventh. The rectory is warm and silent and the light through the front window is the flat grey of a winter afternoon, and you have, for the first time since Advent began, nothing at all to do. Every family in {parish} is at a table. Three of them invited you, at the door, in the way people do, sincerely and without expecting yes. Your own family is what it is, and where it is, and the phone would reach it or would not. There is the plate. There is the television, which {@pastor} leaves on the channel with the fire. There is the class group message, which has gone quiet because everyone is at a table too. You did not expect to feel this. You had thought that the morning, which was full and bright and exhausting and holy, was the whole of Christmas, and it was, and it is now one o'clock, and there are eleven hours of the day left.
events.flavorPrompt: Christmas afternoon in an empty rectory after five Masses. The loneliness of the day after the work of the day. Domestic, exact, no self-pity.

choices.label: Call {@parishioner} back and say yes to the table
choices.outcome: There are nineteen people at the table and a child who wants to sit next to the priest, and the food is the food of a family that has cooked the same things for sixty years, and you are asked to say grace and then are, for three hours, not asked to be anything. You leave at six with a container of leftovers. You have been fed by the people you feed, and the parish, which learns everything, learns that its priest came when asked.

choices.label: Drive to whichever classmate's rectory is closest and has the light on
choices.outcome: {@closest_classmate} is doing what you were doing, in a rectory forty minutes away, and the two of you eat both plates and watch the channel with the fire and say almost nothing about anything that matters, and it is enough. It becomes a thing. Next year there are four of you, and the year after, six, and the chancery hears that the young priests have a Christmas of their own, and is not sure what to make of it.

choices.label: Eat the plate, sleep until dark, and say Evening Prayer
choices.outcome: You sleep four hours in the chair and wake in the dark with the fire on the television and the taste of the pine in the house. You say Vespers for the Nativity alone in the chapel with one candle, and it is, you find, exactly as holy as the morning, and quieter, and you are not sure whether you are at peace or merely too tired to be anything else. It is Christmas. You are a priest. This is what the afternoon is.

choices.label: Call home, whatever home is, and stay on the line as long as it lasts
choices.outcome: The call lasts an hour and the phone is passed around a table three hours away and you hear the sounds of a house you grew up in and a dinner you are not at, and somebody's child says Merry Christmas Father and means the title and the uncle at once. It does not fix the afternoon. It reminds you that you were, before you were this, somebody's, and that the somebody is still there, at a table, keeping a chair.

events.title: Good Friday, three o'clock
events.body: {@pastor}'s back went on Wednesday, at the chrism Mass, and he is upstairs on a heating pad and will do the Vigil if he can stand, which he cannot. You have not slept since Wednesday in any way that counts. Holy Thursday was yours: the Mass, the washing of feet, the procession, the altar of repose until midnight, and the confessions after. It is Good Friday, three o'clock, the hour, and you are in the sacristy in an alb with the Passion to be sung and the veneration of the cross and the Communion service, and after it there are the Stations the parish adds at seven, and tomorrow there is the blessing of the food baskets and the Vigil, which is two and a half hours and has four baptisms and a fire that you have never lit alone. Your hands are not quite steady. There is a thing in your chest that is either grief for the day or something else. The church is full. The deacon is nervous. You could cut something. You could call someone. You could do it all, which is what the parish assumes, and what {@pastor} would have done, and what he is upstairs on a heating pad for having done.
events.flavorPrompt: Holy Week with the pastor down and everything on the vicar. Good Friday afternoon, the body at its limit, the Vigil tomorrow. The hardest week of the year; something has to give.

choices.label: Do all of it. It is Holy Week and there is no one else.
choices.outcome: You sing the Passion and your voice holds. The Stations at seven are said. The Vigil fire lights on the second try and the four baptisms are done and the Exsultet is sung, badly, by you, because there was no one else. Easter Sunday you say three Masses and preach the same homily at all three and it is a good homily. On Easter Monday you cannot get out of bed, and do not, and {@secretary} cancels the day, and the parish speaks of that Triduum for years.

choices.label: Cut the Stations, hand the food blessing to the deacon, and keep what only a priest can do
choices.outcome: The Stations at seven are announced as cancelled from the pulpit at three, and the church is unhappy in the way a church is unhappy about a thing it has always done. The deacon blesses the baskets and is proud. You sleep five hours on Friday and the Vigil is, because you are present for it, the best you have done. The parish forgives the Stations by Pentecost, mostly. You have learned the thing {@pastor} never did, which is where the line is.

choices.label: Call {@brother_priest} and ask him to take the Vigil, or half of it
choices.outcome: He has his own Vigil, and comes anyway, at nine, after it, and does the baptisms and the Eucharistic prayer while you sit in the presider's chair for the first time in three days and let another man's voice fill the church. The parish is bemused and grateful. He will not let you thank him. The presbyterate hears that the vicar at {parish} asked for help in Holy Week, and is of two minds about it, and one of the minds is the right one.

events.title: The vicar for clergy would like a word
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} does not usually come to the parish. He called to say he would be in the area on Thursday and would like to buy you lunch. The lunch is at a place two towns over where no one will know either of you, which is a choice. He orders, and asks about the parish, and then says that someone has spoken to him, and does not say who, and that what they said was that you have not taken a day off in a long time and that you have been preaching the same funeral homily for a season and that you look, in the words of the someone, like a man who is about to walk into a wall. He says he has seen it in better men than either of you. He says {diocese} has a house it uses, and a program, and that two weeks in it now is a better bargain than six months in it later. It is the kind of offer that is written down whether it is taken or not. You have not, until this lunch, said aloud to anyone that anything is wrong. You are sure that someone thought so, and told the chancery, and that you did not see it coming.
events.flavorPrompt: The burnout thread resolves: the vicar for clergy names it over lunch, kindly and on the record. Institutional care with a file attached. Resolve it.

choices.label: Take the two weeks
choices.outcome: The house is quiet and the program is mostly sleep and a counselor who has seen a hundred priests and is not impressed by any of them, which is restful. You come back and the parish says you look well. It is in the file that you went and that you went willingly, and the second part is the part {@vicar_for_clergy} underlines, and it will do you no harm with the men who matter and a little, for a while, with the men who do not.

choices.label: Say you are fine, and that the someone was wrong
choices.outcome: He accepts it, because it is your word and he has no other, and pays, and says to call him. It is in the file that the offer was made and declined. You go back to the parish and take a Monday, the first in months. The wall the someone described is still there. You have decided to be the kind of priest who walks into it standing up, which is a kind, and the diocese has a necrology full of them.

choices.label: Tell him the whole of it, including the nights and the homilies, and let him decide
choices.outcome: It takes the rest of the lunch and he does not interrupt. At the end he says that he will not send you to the house, because a man who can say all that does not need it yet, and that he will instead call {@pastor} about the funerals, and that you will see someone monthly, and that he will know if you do not. It is the most a chancery official has ever done for you and it is also, exactly, supervision, and you have consented to it.

choices.label: Ask him, since he is here, for a different parish
choices.outcome: He is not surprised, and he does not say yes, and he does not say no; he says that a man who asks to move because he is tired is usually tired in the next place too, and that he will remember that you asked. You drive back to {parish} having told the chancery that the problem is the parish, which the chancery will believe about half, and having told yourself the same, which you will believe about the same.

events.title: The hospital calls the rectory
events.body: The hospital calls the rectory at six in the morning, and {@secretary} is not in yet, so it is {@pastor} who takes it and comes to your door in his bathrobe. {@mother} fell in the night. The hip is broken and will be pinned, and the recovery is what it is at her age, which is that she will not go back to living as she was, in an apartment or a house or a rectory room, and the social worker would like to talk to the family today about what comes next. You are the family. There is the rehabilitation place, and after it the place after that, which has a waiting list and a monthly figure that a parochial vicar's salary does not reach. There is the diocese, which has no policy about priests' mothers and a vicar general who might be asked. There is {@pastor}, in the doorway in his bathrobe, who has said nothing yet. There is the seven o'clock Mass in forty minutes, and the parish, and the school, and the fact that you have been doing this for a year now and it has not been a year in which anything else got done well. She is in the third bed on the left and she asked, the nurse says, for Father.
events.flavorPrompt: The mother's decline resolves: a fall, a hip, and the question of what comes next for a priest who is her only family. Practical and tender; resolve the thread.

choices.label: Take the place with the waiting list, and find the money somehow
choices.outcome: The money is found, from a savings account and a brother priest who will not be repaid and the diocese, which turns out to have a fund for things it has no policy for. She goes to the place and hates it and is well cared for. You visit on Mondays, which are yours again, mostly. She is safe and you are a priest again, and you have put your mother in a home, which is what the parish, with sympathy, calls it.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor}, in the doorway, whether she can come here
choices.outcome: He says yes before you finish asking, which tells you what the year has been for him too. The ground-floor room becomes hers, with a hospital bed the Knights find and an aide the altar society organizes without being asked. The parish takes her over. The presbyterate finds it strange and says so. You have a mother in the rectory and a parish that has decided she is theirs, and you will leave here, when you leave, with a problem no assignment board has a box for.

choices.label: Ask {@bishop} for a leave to care for her, and mean it
choices.outcome: {@bishop} does not grant the leave. He grants something else: three months of reduced duties, a supply priest for the Sundays, It is in the file that you asked. It is in the file that he did not say no. You spend the spring in a hospital room and a rehabilitation place, and say Mass at her bedside on Sundays for the two of you, and the parish waits, and the chancery has taken your measure, and is not sure yet what it took.
